text:
Roguing is the process of walking a seed-multiplication field and physically removing undesirable off-type plants so the harvested seed stays true to its variety. It is described as an essential step in seed multiplication, though the source is candid that roguing has limits: how well it works depends partly on how visually distinct the off-type plants are and on the skill of the person doing the roguing. A tall or early-maturing plant stands out clearly in a short or late-maturing variety, but the same kind of difference is much harder to see in the opposite situation (a short plant hiding inside a tall variety), so roguing catches obvious contamination more reliably than subtle contamination.

Why off-types show up in a seed crop even when starting from good seed: the source lists five causes — the variety not being fully homozygous yet, so it is still segregating into slightly different types; the cultivar gradually degenerating from repeated multiplication over many generations; impurity already present in the seed lot; volunteer plants sprouting from a previous crop grown in the same field; and outright mutation.

Roguing should be done several times across the season, at different growth stages, since different off-type traits only become visible at certain stages: tillering, flowering, and maturity are the three stages named. The source's own suggestion is that the single best time to rogue, if only one pass is possible, is at heading (flowering), because that is when plant height is at its maximum (making height differences easiest to see) and when it is easiest to tell early-maturing plants apart from late-maturing ones in the same field.

Traits to check for when identifying an off-type plant to remove: plant height; heading time; leaf, culm, and grain color; leaf angle; panicle exsertion (how far the panicle emerges from the flag-leaf sheath); panicle type; flag-leaf angle; grain size; and presence or absence of awns.

Practical record-keeping tip from the source: record the flowering date of the plot, using 75-80% of plants flowering as the reference point for timing later steps such as roguing passes, harvest planning, and seed-quality decisions.
